questions.problem:
Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}-8\lambda {y}^{′}+16{\lambda }^{2}y=0,\,{y}^{′}(1)=0,\,y(2)+2{y}^{′}(2)=0,\,1\le x\le 2,\,\lambda \in R.
$$

Find the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of this problem. Assume that $B$ and $C$ are constants.

$\,$ The eigenvalues are $\lambda =$ {{field-1}}.

$\,$ The eigenfunctions are $y=$ {{field-2}}.
questions.worked_solution:
We consider the cases $\lambda =0$ and $\lambda \ne 0$ separately, since they correspond to different solutions. 

**Case 1**: First, we consider $\lambda =0.$ 

Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation

$$
{y}^{″}=0.
$$

Integrating this equation gives

$$
y=Ax+B.
$$

Applying the conditions ${y}^{′}(1)=0$ and $y(2)+2{y}^{′}(2)=0$ yields the trivial solution $y≡0.$ Since the zero solution is not an eigenfunction, $\lambda =0$ is not an eigenvalue.

**Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda \ne 0.$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}-8\lambda m+16{\lambda }^{2} & =0 \\ (m-4\lambda )(m-4\lambda ) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the double root $m=4\lambda .$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={e}^{4\lambda x},\,{y}_{2}(x)=x{e}^{4\lambda x}
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y=A{e}^{4\lambda x}+Bx{e}^{4\lambda x}.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =4A\lambda {e}^{4\lambda x}+B{e}^{4\lambda x}+4B\lambda x{e}^{4\lambda x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(1)=0$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}4A\lambda {e}^{4\lambda }+B{e}^{4\lambda }+4B\lambda {e}^{4\lambda } & =0 \\ 4A\lambda +B+4B\lambda  & =0 \\ (4\lambda )A+(1+4\lambda )B & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the boundary condition $y(2)+2{y}^{′}(2)=0$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}A{e}^{8\lambda }+2B{e}^{8\lambda }+2(4A\lambda {e}^{8\lambda }+B{e}^{8\lambda }+8B\lambda {e}^{8\lambda }) & =0 \\ A+2B+2(4A\lambda +B+8B\lambda ) & =0 \\ A+2B+8A\lambda +2B+16B\lambda  & =0 \\ (1+8\lambda )A+(4+16\lambda )B & =0 \\ (1+8\lambda )A+4(1+4\lambda )B & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following systems of equations for $A$ and $B:$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}(4\lambda )A+(1+4\lambda )B=0 \\ (1+8\lambda )A+4(1+4\lambda )B=0\end{aligned}
$$

This homogeneous linear system has a nontrivial solution if and only if the determinant is zero. This gives

$$
|\begin{aligned}4\lambda  & 1+4\lambda  \\ 1+8\lambda  & 4(1+4\lambda )\end{aligned}|=0.
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4\lambda \cdot 4(1+4\lambda )-(1+4\lambda )(1+8\lambda ) & =0 \\ (1+4\lambda )[16\lambda -(1+8\lambda )] & =0 \\ (1+4\lambda )[16\lambda -1-8\lambda ] & =0 \\ (1+4\lambda )(8\lambda -1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{4}\text{ and }{\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{8}.$

Finally, we find the eigenfunction corresponding to each eigenvalue:

- Consider ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{4}.$ Then, we have the solution

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}(x) & =A{e}^{4{\lambda }_{1}x}+Bx{e}^{4{\lambda }_{1}x} \\  & =A{e}^{-x}+Bx{e}^{-x}\end{aligned}
$$

and substituting ${\lambda }_{1}$ into

$$
(4\lambda )A+(1+4\lambda )B=0
$$

 
we get 

$$
-A+(1-1)B=0
$$

 
which gives $A=0,$ and where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is

$$
{y}_{1}(x)=Bx{e}^{-x}.
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{8},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =A{e}^{4{\lambda }_{2}x}+Bx{e}^{4{\lambda }_{2}x} \\  & =A{e}^{x/2}+Bx{e}^{x/2}\end{aligned}
$$

and substituting ${\lambda }_{2}$ into

$$
(4\lambda )A+(1+4\lambda )B=0
$$

 
we get 

$$
\frac{1}{2}A+\frac{3}{2}B=0\,⇒\,A=-3B
$$

where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =-3B{e}^{x/2}+Bx{e}^{x/2} \\  & =B{e}^{x/2}(x-3) \\  & =C{e}^{x/2}(x-3)\end{aligned}
$$

where we have set $C=B.$

So, the eigenfunctions corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively, are $Bx{e}^{-x}\text{ and }C{e}^{x/2}(x-3).$

questions.problem:
Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}-14\lambda {y}^{′}+49{\lambda }^{2}y=0,\,y(0)=0,\,y(2)+{y}^{′}(2)=0,\,0\le x\le 2,\,\lambda \in R.
$$

Find the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of this problem. Assume that $B$ and $C$ are constants.

$\,$ The eigenvalues are $\lambda =$ {{field-1}}.

$\,$ The eigenfunctions are $y=$ {{field-2}}.
questions.worked_solution:
We consider the cases $\lambda =0$ and $\lambda \ne 0$ separately, since they correspond to different solutions. 

**Case 1**: First, we consider $\lambda =0.$ 

Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation

$$
{y}^{″}=0.
$$

Integrating this equation gives

$$
y=Ax+B.
$$

Applying the conditions $y(0)=0$ and $y(2)+{y}^{′}(2)=0$ yields the trivial solution $y≡0.$ Since the zero solution is not an eigenfunction, $\lambda =0$ is not an eigenvalue.

**Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda \ne 0.$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}-14\lambda m+49{\lambda }^{2} & =0 \\ (m-7\lambda )(m-7\lambda ) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the double root $m=7\lambda .$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={e}^{7\lambda x},\,{y}_{2}(x)=x{e}^{7\lambda x}
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y=A{e}^{7\lambda x}+Bx{e}^{7\lambda x}.
$$

Applying the boundary condition $y(0)=0$ yields

$$
A+B\cdot 0=0
$$

which gives $A=0.$ So, we have

$$
y=Bx{e}^{7\lambda x}.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}=B{e}^{7\lambda x}+7B\lambda x{e}^{7\lambda x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the boundary condition $y(2)+{y}^{′}(2)=0$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}2B{e}^{14\lambda }+B{e}^{14\lambda }+14B\lambda {e}^{14\lambda } & =0 \\ 3B{e}^{14\lambda }+14B\lambda {e}^{14\lambda } & =0 \\ B{e}^{14\lambda }+\frac{14}{3}B\lambda {e}^{14\lambda } & =0 \\ B{e}^{14\lambda }(1+\frac{14}{3}\lambda ) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

For nontrivial solutions, we require $B\ne 0.$ Thus, since ${e}^{14\lambda }>0,$ we must have

$$
\lambda =-\frac{3}{14}.
$$

Therefore, the corresponding eigenfunction is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & =Bx{e}^{7\lambda x} \\  & =Bx{e}^{-\frac{3}{2}x}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
We consider the cases $\lambda =0$ and $\lambda \ne 0$ separately, since they correspond to different solutions. 

**Case 1**: First, we consider $\lambda =0.$ 

Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation

$$
{y}^{″}=0.
$$

Integrating this equation gives

$$
y=Ax+B.
$$

Applying the conditions ${y}^{′}(1)=0$ and $y(2)+2{y}^{′}(2)=0$ yields the trivial solution $y≡0.$ Since the zero solution is not an eigenfunction, $\lambda =0$ is not an eigenvalue.

**Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda \ne 0.$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}-20\lambda m+100{\lambda }^{2} & =0 \\ (m-10\lambda )(m-10\lambda ) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the double root $m=10\lambda .$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={e}^{10\lambda x},\,{y}_{2}(x)=x{e}^{10\lambda x}
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y=A{e}^{10\lambda x}+Bx{e}^{10\lambda x}.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =10A\lambda {e}^{10\lambda x}+B{e}^{10\lambda x}+10B\lambda x{e}^{10\lambda x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(1)=0$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}10A\lambda {e}^{10\lambda }+B{e}^{10\lambda }+10B\lambda {e}^{10\lambda } & =0 \\ 10A\lambda +B+10B\lambda  & =0 \\ (10\lambda )A+(1+10\lambda )B & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the boundary condition $y(2)+2{y}^{′}(2)=0$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}A{e}^{20\lambda }+2B{e}^{20\lambda }+2(10A\lambda {e}^{20\lambda }+B{e}^{20\lambda }+20B\lambda {e}^{20\lambda }) & =0 \\ A+2B+2(10A\lambda +B+20B\lambda ) & =0 \\ A+2B+20A\lambda +2B+40B\lambda  & =0 \\ (1+20\lambda )A+(4+40\lambda )B & =0 \\ (1+20\lambda )A+4(1+10\lambda )B & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following systems of equations for $A$ and $B:$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}(10\lambda )A+(1+10\lambda )B=0 \\ (1+20\lambda )A+4(1+10\lambda )B=0\end{aligned}
$$

This homogeneous linear system has a nontrivial solution if and only if the determinant is zero. This gives

$$
|\begin{aligned}10\lambda  & 1+10\lambda  \\ 1+20\lambda  & 4(1+10\lambda )\end{aligned}|=0.
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}10\lambda \cdot 4(1+10\lambda )-(1+10\lambda )(1+20\lambda ) & =0 \\ (1+10\lambda )[40\lambda -(1+20\lambda )] & =0 \\ (1+10\lambda )[40\lambda -1-20\lambda ] & =0 \\ (1+10\lambda )(20\lambda -1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{10}\text{ and }{\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{20}.$

Finally, we find the eigenfunction corresponding to each eigenvalue:

- Consider ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{10}.$ Then, we have the solution

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}(x) & =A{e}^{10{\lambda }_{1}x}+Bx{e}^{10{\lambda }_{1}x} \\  & =A{e}^{-x}+Bx{e}^{-x}\end{aligned}
$$

and substituting ${\lambda }_{1}$ into

$$
(10\lambda )A+(1+10\lambda )B=0
$$

 
we get 

$$
-A+(1-1)B=0
$$

 
which gives $A=0,$ and where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is

$$
{y}_{1}(x)=Bx{e}^{-x}.
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{20},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =A{e}^{10{\lambda }_{2}x}+Bx{e}^{10{\lambda }_{2}x} \\  & =A{e}^{x/2}+Bx{e}^{x/2}\end{aligned}
$$

and substituting ${\lambda }_{2}$ into

$$
(10\lambda )A+(1+10\lambda )B=0
$$

 
we get 

$$
\frac{1}{2}A+\frac{3}{2}B=0\,⇒\,A=-3B
$$

where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =-3B{e}^{x/2}+Bx{e}^{x/2} \\  & =B{e}^{x/2}(x-3) \\  & =C{e}^{x/2}(x-3)\end{aligned}
$$

where we have set $C=B.$

So, the eigenfunctions corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively, are $Bx{e}^{-x}\text{ and }C{e}^{x/2}(x-3).$

Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}+16{\lambda }^{2}y=0,\,{y}^{′}(0)={y}^{′}(\pi )=0,\,0\le x\le \pi ,\,\lambda \ge 0.
$$

Find the parameter values corresponding to the eigenvalues and the associated eigenfunctions of this problem.

$\,$ The eigenvalues correspond to the parameter values ${\lambda }_{n}=$ {{field-1}}, where $n\in N.$

$\,$ The eigenfunctions are ${y}_{n}(x)=$ {{field-2}}, where ${B}_{n}\in R.$
questions.worked_solution:
We consider the cases $\lambda =0$ and $\lambda \ne 0$ separately, since they correspond to different solutions. 

**Case 1**: First, we consider $\lambda =0.$ 

Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation

$$
{y}^{″}=0.
$$

Integrating this equation gives

$$
y=Ax+B.
$$

Applying the conditions ${y}^{′}(0)={y}^{′}(\pi )=0$ yields $A=0.$ Thus, we have a nontrivial solution, so $\lambda =0$ is a parameter value corresponding to the eigenvalue.

**Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda >0.$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}+16{\lambda }^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have $m=\pm 4\text{i}\lambda .$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\lambda x),\,{y}_{2}(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\lambda x)
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\lambda x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\lambda x).
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
{y}^{′}=-4A\lambda \operatorname{sin}⁡(4\lambda x)+4B\lambda \operatorname{cos}⁡(4\lambda x).
$$

Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(0)=0$ yields

$$
-4A\lambda \operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+4B\lambda \operatorname{cos}⁡(0)=0
$$

which gives $B=0.$ So, we have

$$
y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\lambda x).
$$

Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(\pi )=0$ yields

$$
-4A\lambda \operatorname{sin}⁡(4\lambda \pi )=0.
$$

For nontrivial solutions, we require 

$$
4\lambda \pi =n\pi 
$$

for $n\in N.$ This gives the parameter values corresponding to the eigenvalues:

$$
{\lambda }_{n}=\frac{n}{4}.
$$

The corresponding eigenfunctions are 

$$
{y}_{n}(x)={B}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4{\lambda }_{n}x),\,{B}_{n}\in R.
$$

Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}+25\lambda y=0,\,{y}^{′}(0)={y}^{′}(\pi )=0,\,0\le x\le \pi ,\,\lambda \ge 0.
$$

Find the parameter values corresponding to the eigenvalues and the associated eigenfunctions of this problem.

$\,$ The eigenvalues correspond to the parameter values ${\lambda }_{n}=$ {{field-1}}, where $n\in N.$

$\,$ The eigenfunctions are ${y}_{n}(x)=$ {{field-2}}, where ${B}_{n}\in R.$
questions.worked_solution:
We consider the cases $\lambda =0$ and $\lambda >0$ separately, since they correspond to different solutions. 

**Case 1**: First, we consider $\lambda =0.$ 

Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation

$$
{y}^{″}=0.
$$

Integrating this equation gives

$$
y=Ax+B.
$$

Applying the conditions ${y}^{′}(0)={y}^{′}(\pi )=0$ yields $A=0.$ Thus, we have a nontrivial solution, so $\lambda =0$ is a parameter corresponding to the eigenvalue.

**Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda >0.$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}+25\lambda  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have $m=\pm 5\text{i}\sqrt{\lambda }.$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x\sqrt{\lambda }),\,{y}_{2}(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x\sqrt{\lambda })
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x\sqrt{\lambda })+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x\sqrt{\lambda }).
$$

Differentiating, we get

$$
{y}^{′}=-5A\sqrt{\lambda }\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x\sqrt{\lambda })+5B\sqrt{\lambda }\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x\sqrt{\lambda }).
$$

Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(0)=0$ yields

$$
-5A\sqrt{\lambda }\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+5B\sqrt{\lambda }\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)=0
$$

which gives $B=0.$ So, we have

$$
y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x\sqrt{\lambda }).
$$

Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(\pi )=0$ yields

$$
-5A\sqrt{\lambda }\operatorname{sin}⁡(5\pi \sqrt{\lambda })=0.
$$

For nontrivial solutions, we require 

$$
5\pi \sqrt{\lambda }=n\pi 
$$

for $n\in N.$ This gives the parameter values corresponding to the eigenvalues:

$$
{\lambda }_{n}=\frac{{n}^{2}}{25}.
$$

The corresponding eigenfunctions are 

$$
{y}_{n}(x)={B}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x\sqrt{{\lambda }_{n}}),\,{B}_{n}\in R.
$$
